q: A company's internal subordinate CA should only ever be able to issue certificates for *.acu-internal.example and nothing else, even if the CA is compromised. Which certificate extension enforces this?
w: Name constraints in the CA's certificate limit which namespaces it can issue for; basic constraints only says whether it's a CA at all.
h: Name constraints is a fence around the CA's yard — it can only plant certs inside the fence.

q: A web server attaches a signed, time-stamped revocation response from the CA to its TLS handshake, so the browser never contacts the CA itself. What is this?
w: The server fetches and "staples" a short-lived OCSP response, which improves privacy and availability.
h: The server brings its own doctor's note, stapled to the badge, freshly dated.

q: Which statement about a stapled OCSP response is TRUE?
o: It is short-lived and the server refreshes it periodically
It stays valid until the certificate expires
It proves the certificate has not expired
It is signed by the web server's own private key
w: OCSP answers revocation status, not expiry, and the CA-signed response is only good for a short window.
h: A stapled note is dated today; tomorrow the server needs a new one.

q: A mobile app pins its API server's key. Why pin the SPKI hash rather than the hash of the whole certificate?
o: The public key can stay the same when the certificate is renewed
The SPKI hash is secret, so attackers can't read it
The SPKI contains the CA's private key
Whole-certificate hashes are not supported by TLS
w: SPKI is the public key plus its algorithm; renewing the cert with the same key keeps the pin valid.
h: Pin the lock, not the paperwork around it — paperwork gets reissued.

q: A corporate TLS inspection firewall decrypts traffic, but one banking app breaks while browsers work fine. What is the MOST likely reason?
o: The app pins the bank's key, and the firewall can't present that key
The firewall's root CA wasn't pushed to the phones
The app uses a self-signed certificate
OCSP stapling is disabled on the firewall
w: The firewall passes chain validation with its trusted root but can't fake the pinned origin key.
h: Gate 1: someone I trust vouches. Gate 2: is it the exact key I expected? Inspection only wins gate 1.

q: How is a digital signature verified?
o: Decrypt the signature with the sender's public key, rehash the data, and compare
Decrypt the data with the sender's private key and compare hashes
Encrypt the data with the receiver's public key and compare
Hash the sender's private key and compare it to the signature
w: The sender encrypted the hash with their private key, so anyone can decrypt it with the public key and compare to a fresh hash.
h: Private key seals the fingerprint; public key opens the seal so you can match fingerprints.

q: A digital signature on a contract PDF provides all of these EXCEPT:
w: Signing proves who and that nothing changed; the document is still readable by anyone.
h: A signature is a wax seal, not an envelope.

q: An organization wants resolvers to detect DNS cache poisoning by verifying that A records really came from the authoritative zone. Which is BEST?
w: DNSSEC signs the zone's records (RRSIG) so a validating resolver can detect tampering; DANE uses that, it doesn't provide it.
h: DNSSEC protects the address book. DANE checks the badge of whoever's at the address.

q: Which DNSSEC record holds the actual signature over a set of DNS records?
w: RRSIG is the signature; DNSKEY holds the zone's public key; DS links to the parent; TLSA is DANE.
h: RR-SIG = the Record's SIGnature.

q: A mail server publishes a TLSA record so sending servers can check that its TLS certificate matches. What does this require to be trustworthy?
o: An MTA-STS policy file over HTTPS
w: DANE's TLSA record is only trustworthy if DNSSEC proves it wasn't spoofed.
h: An unsigned TLSA record is a badge photo anyone could have swapped.

q: A company can't deploy DNSSEC but wants sending mail servers to require valid TLS when delivering to it. Which is BEST?
w: MTA-STS publishes the TLS policy over HTTPS, using the public CA system instead of DNSSEC.
h: MTA-STS = the STS rules posted on a website, no DNSSEC needed.

q: DNSSEC is deployed. What does it NOT provide?
w: DNSSEC signs but doesn't encrypt; DoH or DoT encrypt queries.
h: DNSSEC is a notarized postcard — trustworthy, but anyone can read it.

q: Employees exchange signed and encrypted email using certificates issued by the company's internal CA. Which technology is this?
w: S/MIME uses X.509 certificates from a CA hierarchy; PGP uses a web of trust.
h: Internal CA in the stem = S/MIME. Web of trust = PGP.

q: DNS logs show one host making thousands of queries for random-looking domains, almost all returning NXDOMAIN. What is MOST likely?
o: Malware using a DGA to find its command-and-control server
w: Mass NXDOMAIN means the malware is still searching for a domain that's actually registered.
h: DGA is knocking on hundreds of doors looking for the one that opens.

q: A host sends many long TXT and subdomain queries like 4a6f686e5f5353.data.badsite.example to one domain. What is MOST likely?
w: Data is being encoded into query names and sent outbound to one attacker-controlled domain.
h: Exfiltration stuffs your files into the envelope's address line.

q: An attacker copies an authorized printer's MAC address so their laptop gets past switch port security. What is the attacker's goal?
w: MAC spoofing is about getting in as a trusted device; interception is ARP poisoning or MAC flooding.
h: MAC spoofing is a fake ID at the door, not a wiretap.

q: A company wants branch traffic steered across broadband and LTE links by application policy, with security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) delivered from the provider's cloud points of presence. What is this?
w: SASE = SD-WAN plus SSE, delivered from the cloud; SD-WAN alone is only the routing half.
h: SASE = SD-WAN + SSE in the cloud. One is the roads, the other is the checkpoints.

q: A retailer wants each store to use two cheap internet links and pick the best path per application, without buying MPLS. Nothing is said about security services. Which is BEST?
w: Path selection across multiple WAN links is SD-WAN; SASE adds cloud security on top.
h: SD-WAN is the smart GPS for your WAN links.

q: Remote contractors need access to one internal app only, verified per session by identity and device health, without being placed on the network. Which is BEST?
w: ZTNA grants per-application access instead of network-level access.
h: VPN gives you the building keys. ZTNA walks you to one room.

q: A firewall must allow an IPsec VPN through NAT. Which ports and protocols are needed?
w: IKE uses UDP 500; NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500. AH (51) breaks under NAT.
h: 500 to start the handshake, 4500 to sneak ESP through NAT.

q: What are IP protocol numbers 50 and 51?
w: ESP is 50, AH is 51 — alphabetical order is backwards from the numbers.
h: ESP comes first (50) because it does more — it encrypts.

q: Which is TRUE about IPsec AH?
o: It provides integrity and authentication but no encryption
It encrypts the payload but not the header
It works through NAT without changes
w: AH authenticates the packet, including parts of the IP header, which is why NAT breaks it.
h: AH = Authentication Header. The name tells you all it does.

q: After IKE Phase 2 completes for one tunnel, how many IPsec SAs exist?
o: Three — IKE plus two data SAs, all from Phase 2
Four — two per peer per direction
w: Phase 1 builds one bidirectional IKE SA; Phase 2 builds two unidirectional IPsec SAs.
h: Phase 2 builds two one-way streets for the data.

q: Two branch firewalls build an IPsec VPN between their LANs, and the original IP headers must be hidden. Which mode?
w: Tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet in a new IP header; aggressive and quick are IKE modes, not IPsec modes.
h: Tunnel mode puts the whole car inside a truck.

q: A company deploys L2TP for remote access with no other protocols. What is the problem?
o: L2TP provides no encryption on its own
w: L2TP is just a tunnel; it's normally paired with IPsec for encryption.
h: L2TP is a pipe with no lock — IPsec is the lock.

q: An attacker records VPN traffic for a year, then steals the gateway's long-term private key. Which feature keeps the old sessions safe?
w: PFS uses a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange per session, so one stolen key doesn't unlock the past.
h: PFS = a new lock every session, so the master key opens nothing old.

q: An attacker captures a valid ESP packet and resends it later. Which feature makes the receiver drop it?
w: ESP sequence numbers let the receiver reject duplicates.
h: Anti-replay is the ticket punch — you can't reuse the same ticket.

q: A defense contractor labels files Secret with compartments, and users need both the clearance level and the compartment to open them. Users can't change labels. Which model?
w: Labels and clearances enforced by the system, not owners, are MAC.
h: MAC = Military-style labels the system enforces. Not "machine."

q: Access is granted only if the user is in Finance, the file is tagged "payroll," and the request comes from a managed device during business hours. Which model?
w: Subject, object, and environment attributes combined is ABAC.
h: ABAC checks the who, the what, and the where/when.

q: A firewall-style policy blocks all logins to the payroll system between 10 PM and 6 AM for everyone, regardless of who they are. Which model?
w: One system-wide rule applied to everyone is rule-based; ABAC evaluates attributes of each subject and object.
h: Rule-based is a sign on the door that applies to everyone.

q: Syslog must be sent to the SIEM encrypted. Which port is used?
w: Syslog over TLS is 6514; plain syslog is 514; 162 is SNMP traps.
h: Secure syslog is the 514 number with a 6 in front.

q: An analyst needs to see which hosts talked to which, over which ports, and how many bytes, without capturing payloads. Which data source?
w: NetFlow is traffic metadata — the phone bill, not the call recording.
h: NetFlow is the phone bill. PCAP is the recording.

q: A SIEM can't correlate events because timestamps across servers are minutes apart. What should be fixed?
w: Correlation depends on consistent clocks.
h: If every witness's watch is wrong, you can't rebuild the timeline.

q: Match the Windows Security Event ID: an account was locked out.
w: 4624 = success, 4625 = failure, 4740 = lockout, 4672 = special privileges.
h: 24 got in, 25 got bounced, 4740 got the door locked.

q: Monitoring must alert when anyone modifies files in C:\Windows\System32 on critical servers. Which tool?
w: FIM hashes and watches critical files for changes.
h: FIM is the tamper seal on the system files.

q: Which statement is correct?
o: MITRE assigns CVE IDs; NIST's NVD adds CVSS scores and CPE names
NIST assigns CVE IDs; MITRE adds CVSS scores
CVSS identifies a vulnerability; CVE scores its severity
CPE is a severity score from 0 to 10
w: CVE = the ID, CVSS = the severity score, CPE = which product/platform it affects.
h: CVE is the name, CVSS is the grade, CPE is the address.

q: In cpe:2.3:a:microsoft:office:2021, what does the "a" mean?
w: CPE part types: a = application, o = operating system, h = hardware.
h: CPE letters: a/o/h = app, OS, hardware.

q: Laptops will be reused inside the company. Per NIST 800-88, which sanitization level is sufficient against simple, non-lab recovery?
w: Clear (logical overwrite) suits in-house reuse; purge resists lab recovery; destroy is physical.
h: Clear = wipe the whiteboard. Purge = repaint it. Destroy = burn it.

q: SSDs leave the company for resale and must resist laboratory recovery while staying usable. Which level?
w: Purge defeats lab techniques without destroying the device.
h: Leaving the building but still working? Purge.

q: Legal tells IT to stop all deletion of a manager's mailbox because a lawsuit is likely. What is this?
w: Legal hold preserves data; e-discovery is later collecting and producing it.
h: Legal hold = freeze. E-discovery = fetch.

q: A policy must stop employees from copying customer SSNs to USB drives, even when the laptop is offline. Which is BEST?
w: Only an agent on the device sees and blocks local copies offline.
h: The USB port is on the laptop, so the guard has to live on the laptop.

q: A bank replaces card numbers with random values in its analytics database; the originals live in a separate secured vault and can be looked up when needed. What is this?
w: Tokens map back to originals through a vault; hashing can't be reversed.
h: Tokenization is a coat-check ticket — useless alone, redeemable at the vault.

q: A European company's cloud data is stored in a U.S. region, so U.S. law can compel access. Which concept is this?
w: Data is subject to the laws of the country where it's stored.
h: Sovereignty: the land owns the rules for what's buried in it.

q: A firewall lets reply traffic back in automatically for connections users started, without a separate inbound rule. What type is it?
w: Stateful firewalls track connections in a state table.
h: Stateful remembers who you called, so it lets their callback through.

q: A device sits in front of the company's web servers, terminates client TLS, caches content, and hides server addresses from the internet. What is it?
w: The test is what it sits in front of: servers = reverse, users = forward.
h: Forward proxy guards your users. Reverse proxy guards your servers.

q: In a zero trust architecture, which component evaluates the request against policy and DECIDES to allow or deny?
w: The Engine decides, the Administrator sets up or tears down the session, the PEP enforces.
h: Engine = judge. Administrator = clerk. PEP = bailiff at the door.

q: A fake AWS access key is planted in a code repository; any attempt to use it triggers an alert. What is this?
w: A fake credential or data record is a honeytoken; a honeyfile is a whole decoy file.
h: Honeytoken = a single marked bill. Honeyfile = a decoy wallet.

q: A change request must document how to restore the system if the firewall upgrade fails. What is this part called?
w: CompTIA's term is backout plan.
h: Back out the way you came in.

q: An asset is worth $200,000. A flood would destroy 25% of it and is expected once every two years. What is the ALE?
h: SLE = AV × EF. ALE = SLE × ARO.

q: ALE before a control is $25,000, ALE after is $5,000, and the control costs $8,000 per year. What is the control's annual value?
h: Savings minus the price tag.

q: A company buys cyber insurance to cover ransomware losses. Which risk treatment?
w: Shifting the financial impact to another party is transfer.
h: Insurance hands the bill to someone else.

q: Security tracks the percentage of unpatched critical servers each month, with a threshold that triggers escalation. What is this metric?
w: A KRI is a metric that warns risk is rising toward tolerance.
h: KRI is the check-engine light.

q: Before acquiring a smaller credit union, the buyer investigates its security posture, audits, and breach history. What is this?
w: Due diligence is the investigation; due care is acting responsibly on what you find.
h: Diligence = Detective work. Care = Carrying it out.

q: A customer wants proof that a SaaS provider's security controls operated effectively over the last 12 months. Which report?
w: Type II covers operating effectiveness over a period; Type I is design at a point in time; SOC 1 is financial reporting.
h: Type I = a photo. Type II = a video.

q: Under PCI DSS 8.3.9, when must user passwords be changed at least every 90 days?
o: When the password is the only authentication factor
w: With MFA (or dynamic risk analysis), forced 90-day rotation isn't required.
h: Password alone? It has to keep changing its disguise.

q: A tester uses Google search operators and Shodan to find a target's exposed login pages. Which kind of reconnaissance is this?
w: No packets hit the target's systems — Google and Shodan receive the queries.
h: Whose systems got the packets? Not the target's = passive.

q: A tester runs Nmap against the target's public IP range to find open ports. Which kind of reconnaissance?
w: Packets are sent directly to the target.
h: You knocked on their door = active.

q: A tabletop exercise walks the team through a ransomware scenario. Which IR phase does this belong to?
w: Exercises, playbooks, and training happen before an incident, in preparation.
h: Practice happens before the game, not during it.

q: A partner's app needs permission to read a user's calendar without ever receiving the user's password. Which protocol?
w: OAuth is delegated authorization with access tokens; SAML is federated authentication for SSO.
h: OAuth = valet key. SAML = passport.

q: Network admins need every command they type on routers authorized and logged individually, with the entire payload encrypted. Which is BEST?
w: TACACS+ separates AAA, supports per-command authorization, and encrypts the whole payload over TCP 49.
h: TACACS+ for Typing on Cisco devices; RADIUS for Reaching the network.
